notes:
1. Goods and Services Tax — Meaning and Core Nature

  • GST stands for Goods and Services Tax.
  • It is an indirect tax levied on the supply of goods or services or both.
  • GST replaced a large number of earlier Union and State indirect taxes.
  • The tax burden generally moves through the supply chain and is ultimately borne by the final consumer.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST → Indirect Tax

2. GST — Tax on Supply

  • The central taxable event under GST is supply*.
  • This replaced the earlier system in which different taxes could depend separately on manufacture, sale or provision of services.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST → Taxable Event = Supply

3. GST — Destination-Based Consumption Tax

  • GST follows destination-based taxation.
  • Revenue broadly accrues to the jurisdiction where final consumption occurs rather than merely where production originates.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST → Destination-Based Tax

4. Destination Principle — Producing vs Consuming State

  • If goods are produced in one State and consumed in another, the State-side GST revenue broadly accrues to the destination State.
  • Production location alone does not determine the final State-side revenue.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GST → Consumption Destination

Not Origin of Production

5. GST — Value-Added Tax Character

  • GST taxes value addition across successive stages of the supply chain.
  • Eligible tax paid at an earlier stage can be credited against tax payable at a later stage through Input Tax Credit.

6. Input Tax Credit — ITC

  • ITC stands for Input Tax Credit.
  • An eligible registered person can claim credit of GST paid on eligible business inputs or input services against output-tax liability, subject to statutory conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

ITC → Input Tax Credit

7. ITC — Main Purpose

  • ITC reduces cascading or tax-on-tax effects.
  • GST is therefore broadly intended to tax incremental value addition rather than repeatedly taxing the entire value at each stage.
📌 Must-Memorise

ITC → Reduces Cascading

8. ITC — Basic Calculation Logic

The broad logic is:

Output GST Liability

− Eligible Input Tax Credit

= Net GST Payable

9. Cascading Effect — Meaning

  • Cascading occurs when a tax is effectively imposed on value that already includes an earlier tax.
  • GST's credit mechanism seeks to minimise this effect.

10. Pre-GST Indirect Tax Structure

Before GST, important indirect taxes included:

  • Central Excise Duty.
  • Service Tax.
  • State VAT.
  • Central Sales Tax.
  • Entry Tax.
  • Luxury Tax.
  • Purchase Tax.
  • Various additional duties and State levies.

11. Why GST Was Introduced

GST sought to address:

  • Multiple indirect taxes.
  • Fragmented administration.
  • Cascading taxation.
  • Breaks in tax-credit chains.
  • Differences in State tax structures.
  • Barriers to a more integrated national market.

12. GST — Common National Market Objective

  • Greater harmonisation of indirect taxation across States supports national market integration.
  • A more uniform tax framework can reduce fiscal barriers between States.

13. Constitutional Amendment — Need

  • GST required constitutional amendment because both the Union and States needed legislative powers over a common tax base involving supply of goods and services.

14. 101st Constitutional Amendment Act — 2016

  • The constitutional framework for GST was created through the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016.
  • Presidential assent was given on 8 September 2016.
📌 Must-Memorise

101st Constitutional Amendment → GST

15. 122nd Amendment Bill — Important Distinction

  • The measure was introduced in Parliament as the Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill.
  • It was introduced in Lok Sabha on 19 December 2014.
  • After enactment, it became the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act*.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

122nd Amendment Bill → 101st Amendment Act

16. GST Implementation — 1 July 2017

  • GST was implemented across India from 1 July 2017*.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Launch → 1 July 2017

17. GST Historical Memory Chain

  • 2014 → 122nd Amendment Bill introduced.
  • 2016 → 101st Constitutional Amendment enacted.
  • 8 September 2016 → Presidential assent.
  • 1 July 2017 → GST implemented.

18. Article 246A — GST Legislative Powers

  • Article 246A provides the special legislative framework for GST.
  • Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate on GST subject to the constitutional framework.
  • Parliament has exclusive power regarding GST on inter-State supplies.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 246A → GST Law-Making Powers

19. Article 269A — Inter-State GST

  • Article 269A deals with GST on inter-State trade or commerce.
  • GST on inter-State supplies is levied and collected by the Union and apportioned under the constitutional framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 269A → Inter-State GST

20. Article 279A — GST Council

  • Article 279A provides for the GST Council.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 279A → GST Council

21. GST Constitutional Chain

  • 101st Amendment → GST constitutional framework.
  • Article 246A → GST legislative power.
  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
📌 Must-Memorise

101st → 246A → 269A → 279A

22. Article 269A vs Article 279A

  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

269A ≠ 279A

23. Dual GST Model

  • India follows a dual GST model.
  • Both Union and States participate in taxing the same broad supply base according to constitutional and statutory rules.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian GST → Dual GST

24. CGST — Central Component

  • CGST means Central Goods and Services Tax.
  • It is the Central component of GST.
  • The Union administers CGST under the GST framework.

25. SGST — State Component

  • SGST means State Goods and Services Tax.
  • It is the State component of GST.
  • The respective State Government administers SGST on applicable intra-State supplies.

26. UTGST — Union Territory Component

  • UTGST means Union Territory Goods and Services Tax.
  • It applies as the Union Territory component in applicable Union Territories without legislatures.

27. IGST — Integrated Goods and Services Tax

  • IGST means Integrated Goods and Services Tax.
  • It applies to inter-State supplies.
  • The Centre levies and administers IGST.
📌 Must-Memorise

Inter-State Supply → IGST

28. Intra-State Supply

  • A taxable intra-State supply generally attracts:
  • CGST.
  • SGST.
📌 Must-Memorise

Intra-State → CGST + SGST

29. Intra-UT Supply

  • In an applicable Union Territory without legislature, an intra-territory supply generally attracts:
  • CGST.
  • UTGST.

30. Inter-State Supply

  • A taxable supply across State boundaries generally attracts IGST.
📌 Must-Memorise

Inter-State → IGST

31. GST Component Memory Chain

  • Intra-State → CGST + SGST.
  • Applicable intra-UT → CGST + UTGST.
  • Inter-State → IGST.

32. IGST — Credit and Settlement Role

  • IGST helps maintain continuity of the input-tax-credit chain across State boundaries.
  • Settlement mechanisms help preserve the destination-based character of GST.

33. Imports — GST Treatment

  • Imports of goods are treated as inter-State supplies for GST purposes.
  • IGST applies in addition to applicable customs duties.
  • Import of services is also treated as inter-State supply.
📌 Must-Memorise

Imports → Inter-State Treatment → IGST

34. Supply — Broad Legal Concept

  • Supply is broader than a simple sale.
  • Sale of goods is one example.
  • GST law also recognises other transactions within the statutory definition of supply.

35. Supply and Consideration

  • Taxable supply commonly involves goods or services supplied for consideration in the course or furtherance of business.
  • GST law also specifies situations where supply can be recognised even without consideration.

36. Inter-State Stock Transfer

  • Inter-State stock transfers between distinct registered establishments can fall within the supply framework even without a conventional sale.

37. ITC — Important Conditions

  • ITC is not unrestricted.
  • It remains subject to statutory eligibility, documentation and other conditions.
  • Eligible invoices, debit notes or bills of entry may be relevant depending on the transaction.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GST Paid ≠ Automatically Unlimited ITC

38. Taxes Subsumed into GST

Important pre-GST taxes absorbed wholly or partly into the GST framework included:

  • Central Excise on GST-covered goods.
  • Service Tax.
  • Additional Excise Duties.
  • CVD.
  • SAD.
  • State VAT on GST-covered supplies.
  • Central Sales Tax within the transition framework.
  • Luxury Tax.
  • Entry Tax.
  • Purchase Tax.
  • Certain entertainment and amusement taxes.
  • Taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling.

39. Service Tax — High-Yield Fact

  • Service Tax was subsumed into GST.
📌 Must-Memorise

Service Tax → Subsumed into GST

40. GST Did Not Replace Every Tax

  • GST did not abolish every Union, State or local tax.
  • Certain products and levies remain outside GST or receive special constitutional treatment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GST ≠ Abolition of All Taxes

41. Alcoholic Liquor for Human Consumption

  • Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside the constitutional GST levy framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alcohol for Human Consumption → Outside GST

42. Five Petroleum Products — Special Treatment

The constitutional GST framework gives special treatment to:

  • Petroleum crude.
  • High-speed diesel.
  • Petrol.
  • Natural gas.
  • Aviation turbine fuel.
📌 Must-Memorise

Crude → Diesel → Petrol → Natural Gas → ATF

43. Tobacco — GST and Excise

  • Tobacco and tobacco products can be subject to GST.
  • Central Excise Duty can also apply under the constitutional framework.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tobacco → GST + Possible Central Excise

44. GST Council — Constitutional Institution

  • GST Council is established under Article 279A.
  • It serves as a joint Union-State forum for GST matters.
  • It is a central institution of cooperative fiscal federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Council → Article 279A

45. GST Council — Constitution and First Meeting

  • GST Council was constituted during the 2016 GST rollout process.
  • Its first meeting was held on 22–23 September 2016.
📌 Must-Memorise

First GST Council Meeting → September 2016

46. GST Council — Chairperson and Members

  • Union Finance Minister → Chairperson.
  • Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance → Member.
  • Each State → Finance/Taxation Minister or another nominated Minister.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Council Chairperson → Union Finance Minister

47. GST Council — Main Functions

The Council makes recommendations on matters such as:

  • GST rates.
  • Exemptions.
  • Thresholds.
  • Taxable goods and services.
  • Place-of-supply principles.
  • Model GST laws.
  • Special rates during disasters.
  • Special provisions for States.

48. GST Council — Quorum

  • One-half of the total number of members constitutes the quorum.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Council Quorum → 1/2

49. GST Council — Voting Weights

  • Union Government → 1/3 of weighted votes.
  • States together → 2/3.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union → 1/3

States → 2/3

50. GST Council — Decision Threshold

  • A decision requires at least three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting when voting takes place.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Council Decision → 3/4 Weighted Majority

51. GST Council — Consensus and Voting

  • The constitutional framework provides a weighted-voting mechanism.
  • In practice, the Council generally attempts to reach decisions through consensus.

52. GST Council Secretariat

  • The GST Council is supported by a Secretariat headquartered in New Delhi.
  • The Secretary, Revenue serves as ex officio Secretary to the Council under the institutional arrangement.

53. CBIC Chairperson — Invitee Role

  • The Chairperson of the Central indirect-tax administration has a permanent invitee role without voting rights in Council proceedings.

54. GST Council — Federal Significance

  • The Council institutionalises joint Union-State participation in indirect-tax policymaking.
  • It is one of India's clearest examples of cooperative fiscal federalism.

55. GST Administration — Centre and States

Centre:

  • Administers CGST.
  • Levies and administers IGST.

States:

  • Administer SGST within their jurisdictions.

56. GST Registration

  • GST law requires registration based on applicable turnover thresholds and specified compulsory-registration categories.
  • Exact limits and exceptions can differ by taxpayer category and statutory provision.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GST Registration Threshold ≠ One Permanent Number for Every Taxpayer

57. PAN and GSTIN

  • GST registration operates through a PAN-linked framework.
  • A registered taxpayer is identified through GSTIN.
📌 Must-Memorise

GSTIN → Goods and Services Tax Identification Number

58. Composition Scheme

  • GST provides a simplified composition mechanism for eligible small taxpayers.
  • Eligibility, turnover limits, rates and restrictions are governed by current law and notifications.
📌 Must-Memorise

Composition Scheme → Simplified Scheme for Eligible Small Taxpayers

59. Regular vs Composition Taxpayer

Regular taxpayer:

  • Normal GST credit and return framework.

Composition taxpayer:

  • Simplified statutory framework.
  • Subject to restrictions and eligibility conditions.

60. Reverse Charge Mechanism — RCM

  • RCM stands for Reverse Charge Mechanism.
  • In specified cases, liability to pay GST shifts from supplier to recipient.
📌 Must-Memorise

RCM → Recipient Pays GST

61. Forward Charge vs Reverse Charge

Normal forward charge:

  • Supplier collects and pays GST.

Reverse charge:

  • Recipient becomes liable in specified cases.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Normal → Supplier

RCM → Recipient

62. GST — Digital Compliance Framework

  • GST relies extensively on electronic registration, filing, invoice information and tax administration.
  • Digital processes can improve standardisation, traceability and compliance.

63. GSTN — Technology Infrastructure

  • India's GST system uses common information-technology infrastructure for taxpayer-facing functions and data exchange.

64. E-Invoice and IRN

  • Under the e-invoice system, prescribed registered persons upload relevant invoice information to an Invoice Registration Portal.
  • An Invoice Reference Number is generated.
📌 Must-Memorise

IRN → Invoice Reference Number

65. E-Way Bill

  • E-Way Bill is an electronic document associated with movement of goods in circumstances covered by GST rules.
  • It can involve registered persons and enrolled transporters.

66. E-Invoice vs E-Way Bill

  • E-Invoice → Invoice authentication.
  • E-Way Bill → Movement of goods.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

E-Invoice ≠ E-Way Bill

67. Place of Supply — Importance

  • Place-of-supply rules help determine whether a transaction is intra-State or inter-State.
  • They also determine the jurisdiction to which GST revenue is attributed.
  • These rules are essential for implementing destination-based taxation.

68. GST Compensation to States Act — 2017

  • Parliament enacted the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017.
  • It created a mechanism to compensate States for specified revenue losses arising from GST implementation.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Compensation to States Act → 2017

69. Original Compensation Framework

  • The original compensation framework covered five years from GST implementation.
  • 2015–16 was used as the base year for subsumed-tax revenue.
  • Protected revenue incorporated an assumed annual growth rate of 14%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Original GST Compensation Growth Assumption → 14%

70. Compensation Cess

  • GST Compensation Cess was created to raise resources for State compensation.
  • It applies to specified supplies under the statutory framework.

71. Major Advantages of GST

Important intended benefits include:

  • Reduced cascading.
  • Wider input-tax-credit chain.
  • Greater tax harmonisation.
  • Improved transparency.
  • Digital administration.
  • Better information matching.
  • Improved compliance.
  • Wider tax base.
  • Greater national-market integration.
  • Improved competitiveness.
  • Cooperative federalism.

72. GST — Compliance and Administrative Challenges

Important challenges include:

  • Registration compliance.
  • Invoicing requirements.
  • Return filing.
  • ITC documentation.
  • Centre-State coordination.
  • Technology dependence.
  • Classification disputes.
  • Policy and rate changes.

73. GST Rates — Important Caution

  • India does not have one identical GST rate for every taxable good or service.
  • Different categories can attract different rates or exemptions.
  • Rates can change through the statutory process following GST Council recommendations.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GST Rate ≠ One Uniform Permanent Rate

74. Exempt vs Taxable Supply

  • Not every supply attracts GST at a positive rate.
  • Exemptions and special treatments are provided through law and notifications.

75. Tamil Nadu — Destination Principle

  • Tamil Nadu receives State-side GST revenue when Tamil Nadu is the destination jurisdiction for taxable consumption under applicable rules.
  • Merely producing goods in Tamil Nadu does not guarantee that Tamil Nadu receives the State-side tax if consumption occurs elsewhere.

76. Producing State vs Consuming State

  • Destination-based GST broadly favours the consuming jurisdiction for State-side revenue.
  • This differs from an origin-based taxation system.

77. GST — Core Institutional Identity

GST =

Indirect Tax

  • Supply-Based
  • Destination-Based
  • Dual GST
  • Input Tax Credit
📌 Must-Memorise

This is the core GST identity chain.

78. GST — Core Constitutional Identity

GST =

101st Amendment

  • Article 246A
  • Article 269A
  • Article 279A

79. GST — Federal Identity

GST =

Union

  • States
  • GST Council
  • Shared Tax Framework

80. Supply Memory Chain

  • Taxable event → Supply.
  • Intra-State → CGST + SGST.
  • Intra-UT → CGST + UTGST.
  • Inter-State → IGST.
  • Imports → Inter-State treatment.

81. Credit Memory Chain

Purchase

→ Input Tax Paid

→ Eligible ITC

→ Output Tax Liability

→ Net GST Payable

82. Council Memory Chain

  • Chairperson → Union Finance Minister.
  • Quorum → 1/2.
  • Union voting weight → 1/3.
  • States together → 2/3.
  • Decision → 3/4 weighted majority.

83. Exclusion Memory Chain

  • Alcohol for human consumption → Outside GST.
  • Five petroleum products → Special constitutional treatment.
  • Tobacco → GST + possible Central Excise.

84. Compliance Memory Chain

  • GSTIN → Registration identity.
  • ITC → Input tax credit.
  • RCM → Recipient liability.
  • E-Invoice → Invoice authentication.
  • IRN → Invoice Reference Number.
  • E-Way Bill → Goods movement.

85. TNPSC Traps

  • GST is an indirect tax.
  • GST was implemented on 1 July 2017.
  • 101st Constitutional Amendment created the GST framework.
  • 122nd Amendment Bill became the 101st Amendment Act.
  • GST is based on supply.
  • GST is destination-based.
  • India follows dual GST.
  • CGST → Central component.
  • SGST → State component.
  • IGST → Inter-State supplies.
  • Intra-State → CGST + SGST.
  • Inter-State → IGST.
  • Imports are treated as inter-State supplies.
  • Article 246A → GST legislative power.
  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
  • Article 269A and 279A are different.
  • GST Council is a constitutional institution.
  • Union Finance Minister chairs it.
  • Quorum → 1/2.
  • Union vote → 1/3.
  • States → 2/3.
  • Decision threshold → 3/4.
  • ITC reduces cascading.
  • ITC is conditional, not automatic.
  • Service Tax was subsumed into GST.
  • State VAT on GST-covered supplies was subsumed.
  • GST did not abolish every tax.
  • Alcohol for human consumption is outside GST.
  • Five petroleum products have special treatment.
  • Tobacco can attract GST and Central Excise.
  • GST favours destination of consumption rather than production origin.
  • GST rates can change.
  • India does not have one single uniform GST rate.
  • Composition levy is for eligible small taxpayers under conditions.
  • RCM → Recipient pays in specified cases.
  • E-Invoice and E-Way Bill are different.
  • E-Invoice → Invoice authentication.
  • E-Way Bill → Goods movement.
  • GST Compensation to States Act → 2017.
  • Original compensation framework → Five years.
  • Protected-revenue growth assumption → 14%.

86. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • GST → Goods and Services Tax.
  • Type → Indirect.
  • Taxable Event → Supply.
  • Nature → Destination-Based.
  • Model → Dual GST.
  • Amendment → 101st.
  • Year → 2016.
  • Launch → 1 July 2017.
  • 246A → GST Powers.
  • 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • 279A → GST Council.
  • Intra-State → CGST + SGST.
  • Inter-State → IGST.
  • ITC → Input Tax Credit.
  • Council Chair → Union Finance Minister.
  • Quorum → 1/2.
  • Union Vote → 1/3.
  • States → 2/3.
  • Decision → 3/4.
  • Alcohol → Outside GST.
  • RCM → Recipient Pays.
  • E-Invoice → IRN.
  • E-Way Bill → Goods Movement.

  • GST full form? → Goods and Services Tax.
  • GST is direct or indirect? → Indirect tax.
  • GST taxable event? → Supply.
  • GST nature? → Destination-based consumption tax.
  • Constitutional Amendment? → 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
  • Amendment Bill number? → 122nd Amendment Bill.
  • GST implemented? → 1 July 2017.
  • Article 246A? → GST legislative powers.
  • Article 269A? → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 279A? → GST Council.
  • GST model in India? → Dual GST.
  • CGST? → Central Goods and Services Tax.
  • SGST? → State Goods and Services Tax.
  • UTGST? → Union Territory Goods and Services Tax.
  • IGST? → Integrated Goods and Services Tax.
  • Intra-State supply? → CGST + SGST.
  • Applicable intra-UT supply? → CGST + UTGST.
  • Inter-State supply? → IGST.
  • Imports treated as? → Inter-State supplies.
  • Destination principle means? → Tax broadly accrues where consumption occurs.
  • ITC full form? → Input Tax Credit.
  • Main ITC purpose? → Reduce cascading.
  • GST Council Article? → 279A.
  • GST Council Chairperson? → Union Finance Minister.
  • Union MoS Revenue/Finance? → Member.
  • State representation? → Finance/Taxation Minister or nominated Minister.
  • GST Council quorum? → One-half.
  • Union voting weight? → One-third.
  • States' collective voting weight? → Two-thirds.
  • Decision threshold? → Three-fourths weighted majority.
  • Who recommends GST rates? → GST Council.

  • GSTIN means? → Goods and Services Tax Identification Number.
